prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and the theory of monetary policy rules.

statement.case_for: The framework of nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and interest-rate rules is the working core of modern monetary policy analysis, and it has been tested over several decades and through two very different macroeconomic episodes. Calvo supplies a tractable time-dependent pricing device. Taylor supplies staggered contracts and the policy rule. Woodford supplies the microfounded, welfare-based synthesis that turned these pieces into a coherent theory of monetary policy. Each is a distinct, identifiable and foundational contribution, and the three together cover the conceptual core rather than the later estimation and extension work. After reading my colleagues' openings, I still judge this to have the longest record of confirmation and the clearest policy consequences among the shortlisted candidates. That record matters more to me than breadth of opening support.
statement.case_against: Credit is the weak point. The ballot lists eight names, and Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler have strong claims that a three-person cap excludes. Several colleagues (Andersson, Boppart, Dreber-Almenberg) make this point, and I accept it. The core of the framework, especially Calvo-style pricing and the representative-agent versions, has also been challenged by micro price data and by the 2021-23 inflation. Related territory has been recognised in earlier macro prizes, so marginal novelty is a fair question. If the Committee will not accept a three-name cut, a cleaner single-mechanism award such as B004 is the better route.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B015 seventh. He regards Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the most defensible three but flags empirical challenges to Calvo-style pricing from micro price data, and he questions whether the field is already rewarded by earlier macro prizes.
responses.response: The empirical concern is serious, and I have to disclose that I co-authored a menu-cost paper with Friberg. State-dependent and asymmetric adjustment evidence does qualify the Calvo device as a literal description of firm behaviour. I do not think it undermines the prize case, though. The contribution is a tractable framework that organised monetary policy analysis and was then refined against micro evidence, including work like ours. I would write the citation around nominal rigidities and policy rules in general rather than around time-dependent pricing alone. That is why the citation is worded broadly. I do not agree that earlier prizes (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims) covered this core. They covered expectations and credibility, not price-setting and rule-based policy design.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B004 first. He sees the collateral-constraint mechanism as foundational, he thinks Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators, and he treats Gertler's overlap with Bernanke (2022) as weakening the case for crediting Gertler.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution logic and have placed B004 second for it. The Kiyotaki-Moore pair is cleaner than anything B015 can offer, and I have already proposed the pair without Gertler for the Bernanke-overlap reason he gives. We differ on two points. First, the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises covers adjacent ground more directly than any earlier prize covers B015, so I give B004 less marginal novelty. Second, a two-name award would leave the financial-accelerator strand uncredited, and the Committee should be explicit about that. I would support B004 if the Committee decides B015 cannot be credited cleanly, but I do not think it is stronger on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first. He emphasises that population-scale administrative data made intergenerational mobility a measurable, place-specific object, with credible quasi-experimental designs, and he notes that the long-run causal claims are still being tested.
responses.response: This is the strongest challenge to my ordering, and I treat it seriously. B002 has the broadest opening support, and I ranked it third on merit. I think the measurement and policy consequences are transformative. My reservations are timing and attribution. The core results are from 2014-2022, causal neighbourhood effects are still debated, and credit is spread across a large team (Chetty, Hendren, Friedman, Katz). I would not oppose B002 in a later year. I place it behind B015 because B015 has decades of confirmation and B002 has not yet had the same test. I should disclose that my own work on intelligence, social mobility and growth is adjacent to the mobility literature, and that may colour how I judge its novelty. I do not treat support counts as scientific evidence in either direction.

uncertainties: Whether a three-name cut of an eight-name field can be defended as a fair attribution, and whether Gali or Christiano-Eichenbaum would be better choices than Calvo or Taylor.
How much weight the post-2021 inflation experience and the micro price-setting evidence should have against a framework whose core is decades old.
Whether B002 is mature enough that its long-run causal neighbourhood claims will hold up, since this would change my relative ordering of it and B015.
My assessments rest on general knowledge of the literature and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile shows several connections that may warrant disclosure and that I do not adjudicate. Per Krusell (committee secretary), who also ranked B015 first, is a frequent co-author and an IIES colleague. I co-authored a menu-costs paper with Richard Friberg, which is adjacent to the price-rigidity theme of B015. I co-authored with Timo Boppart. My own social-mobility research is adjacent to B002. None of the proposed B015 laureates (Taylor, Woodford, Calvo) is named in the supplied profile as a co-author or institutional connection.
